content: In younger adolescents aged 10 to 14 years, the recommendation for voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) was considered conditional due to limited evidence regarding its use in this age group. The broader discussion of offering VMMC to this demographic, using any clinical method, is detailed in Chapter 3. Chapter 3.1 also presents GRADE tables, summaries of studies, and evidence profile tables. Each circumcision device has unique characteristics, and a detailed quality assessment for each outcome by device type—including the collar clamp, elastic collar compression device, and surgical assist vice clamp device—is provided in the annex. Most clinical studies on circumcision devices for potential use in VMMC programs classified adverse event (AE) severity consistently. AEs manageable by mid-level clinicians within the VMMC program were considered moderate, while those requiring immediate surgical intervention by an experienced specialist or referral to higher-level care were classified as severe. Evidence for recommendations focused on two types of in situ devices—a collar clamp device and an elastic collar compression device—and one surgical assist device. Further evidence is needed to demonstrate the safety and advantages of these devices, particularly in adolescents, when scaled in routine healthcare settings. The quality of data on the efficacy, safety, and acceptability of these devices was considered low due to indirectness and risk of bias, as neither patients nor observers were blinded. A systematic review identified publications and reports on the safety, efficacy, and acceptability of the collar clamp device. Twelve studies on the conventional placement technique, involving 3,535 clients in Africa, and three studies on the no-flip method with 654 participants were conducted. This evidence, relevant to VMMC programs for HIV prevention in East and Southern Africa, was supported by studies from China. Eligibility studies in Africa reported that 6% of eligible men (55 out of 3,377) could not undergo circumcision with the collar clamp device due to the unavailability of the correct ring size. No additional exclusions were reported. In studies using the no-flip method, no clients were excluded. The no-flip technique, developed in China, simplifies device placement by avoiding foreskin eversion over the ring's exterior. Circumcision was successfully achieved in nearly all clients where device placement was attempted, with a low failure rate of 3 per 1,000 placements. Failures were attributed to device slippage, healthcare worker inexperience, foreskin damage, insufficient foreskin for eversion, or thick foreskin preventing ring closure. Most failures occurred during initial use at new sites or in adolescents. With the no-flip technique, only one placement failure occurred out of 664 procedures in Africa, due to outer ring slippage after device application and foreskin removal. In all cases, wounds were closed using sutures. Adverse events (AEs) were assessed in terms of the number of clients experiencing severe or moderate AEs, regardless of type or cause. Severe AEs included events requiring prompt surgical intervention, while moderate AEs were manageable by mid-level clinicians. The overall AE rate was 7%, with 4% classified as severe. Pain levels during and after the procedure were similar to those reported with conventional surgery. Oedema and hematoma were less common with the collar clamp device compared to conventional surgery. Limited evidence was available on infections, with a reported rate of 2.6% (17 out of 654 clients). Severe pain, bleeding after device placement, and wound dehiscence were among the reported AEs. Healing time following circumcision with the collar clamp device was approximately one week longer than after conventional surgery. Healing occurred by secondary intention rather than primary intention, as in surgical circumcision where wound edges are approximated with sutures. In randomized studies, healing took about five days longer with the collar clamp device, with 86% of clients healed at six weeks. The no-flip technique showed slightly shorter healing times, potentially due to the younger age of clients in those studies. A small number of wound disruptions (<1%) occurred weeks after device removal, representing deviations from the normal healing process. Pain during device placement and the post-procedure period was comparable to conventional surgery. The collar clamp device avoids the need for sutures for hemostasis and clamps the skin edges firmly to facilitate healing. Local anesthesia is required before device placement due to the tight clamping mechanism and foreskin removal. Some men reported pain while wearing the device and higher pain levels during erections compared to conventional surgery. Evidence on pain with the no-flip method was of very low quality. Topical anesthesia, compared to injectable local anesthesia, required longer wait times to prevent pain during the procedure, and 27% of clients with adhesions or phimosis required supplementary injectable anesthesia. The elastic collar compression device, specifically the PrePex™ device, was studied in 21 studies involving 12,855 clients. The foreskin and device were removed seven days after placement in the Day 7 removal procedure. Five studies involving 1,254 clients used a modified Day 0 foreskin removal procedure, where the foreskin was excised within hours of device placement, followed by device removal after seven days. This modification aimed to address odor and discomfort associated with necrotizing foreskin and reduce the risk of tetanus infection. However, as of 2020, evidence was uncertain regarding whether this modification reduced tetanus risk. Adverse events with the elastic collar compression device included severe and moderate AEs, with rates varying between 4% and 12% across studies. Severe AEs, such as severe edema requiring management by experienced surgeons, were rare but successfully treated without long-term sequelae. Cases of tetanus, considered serious AEs, were reported with the elastic collar compression device. WHO advised ensuring tetanus toxoid-containing vaccine (TTCV) protection before using this method. Client satisfaction with the cosmetic result of circumcision was high, with 92% of clients reporting being satisfied or very satisfied with penile appearance. In adolescents, 96% expressed high satisfaction with the elastic collar compression procedure. Return to daily activities was generally quicker with the elastic collar compression device compared to conventional surgery. However, some men reported transient discomfort or pain during device removal. A small proportion of clients (8%) reported an unpleasant smell while wearing the device, which affected their daily activities.
